maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA VEGETABLE GROWERS
BRITISH COLUMBIA VEGETABLE GROWERS

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA VEGETABLE GROWERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have in my hand a letter from the firm of Hayward and Scott, wholesale produce and commission merchants, Vancouver, B.C., in connection with the export of vegetables to the British troops in China. I will not take up the time of the House by reading it all, but I wish to read this extract:
We notice Mr. Tolmie's inquiry and reply of Mr. Motherwell as to why white dealers and growers had no opportunity of quoting on potatoes supplied to the British forces in China.
We understand these orders were placed by Mr. Clarke who is the Dominion fruit inspector in Vancouver. The business was given to R. Robertson Company, and two shipments were made-R. Robertson Company shipping the first orders-buying both potatoes and onions from Chinese dealers. White dealers and growers had no opportunity of quoting on the first order. There were hundreds of tons of potatoes available in the hands of white dealers and growers, had they been given an opportunity to quote. The second order for potatoes which went forward on the last Canadian Pacific boat, Empress of Canada, sailing from Vancouver February 26, was also filled by R. Robertson Company.
The onions on the second order were supplied by Fraser-Wood Company. Some of the dealers heard this second order was being placed and called up Mr. Clarke, but received no encouragement from him-evidently it was a cut and dried proposition that Robertson Company was to receive this order-Fraser-Wood, however, brought a little influence to bear through Ottawa, and received the onion order.
This statement by Mr. Clarke and Mr. Robertson that it was impossible to supply potatoes and onions from white growers, is absolutely untrue, and also the statement that the time was too short to secure these goods, is also wrong. R. Robertson Company are brokers who do not carry any stocks. It may have been difficult for them to supply goods, but other dealers and growers who carry a stock on hand would have had no difficulty in filling these orders.
R. Robertson Company had the goods put up by Chinamen and these potatoes were grown by Chinamen. Messrs. Motherwell, Clarke and Robertson's assertions that white dealers and growers were unable to supply these goods is untrue.
There are thousands of tons of potatoes both in Vancouver and the adjoining districts grown by white growers and these could have been supplied, had they been given an opportunity of quoting. It surely does not look very consistent to have the Chinese supplying the ammunition to fight the Chinamen in China.
We are enclosing copy of a picture taken on the wharf showing these goods being delivered by the Chinese dealer in Vancouver.

Vermilion Wheat
I have also a picture of the dock showing a large number of potatoes in sacks, a truck loaded with potatoes alongside, with a Chinese chauffeur, and on the side of the truck appears the name Wong Fat. Has the minister any further information on this question?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA VEGETABLE GROWERS
speechtext:
If my hon. friend had given
me an opportunity I might have had the documentary evidence with me. The first offer to fill this order for potatoes and onions was given, so far as my recollection goes, to a firm in the Okanagan valley, but they had not the goods and therefore we had to look for supplies elsewhere. We have not inquired into the colour of Mr. Robertson-I mean the colour of his skin, nor the colour of his politics, but I presume he is white. It never, however, occurred to me to inquire into the nationality of the growers who supplied these potatoes to Mr. Robertson. The second offer to have this order filled was given to Mr. Robertson as a responsible broker and I assume he got them where he liked as long as he complied with the conditions of the contract. There was only one thing upon which the British authorities, through the High Commissioner's office, insisted, and that was that all these goods would be examined carefully by the government inspector and that they must be of the proper quality. That condition was complied with. As regards the statement that some of these growers who supplied the goods to Mr. Robertson were Chinamen, that may be so. I do not know; I assume it is so; but when the overseas authorities wore buying wheat from the western provinces during the war I do not think anybody ever thought of asking who grew the wheat or what colour was the skin of the man who grew it. I do not want to magnify this or to make light of it; but with the Empress of Asia lying in the harbour scheduled to sail on a given date seven or eight days after the first communication, if the goods were not supplied on time and up to quality, the boat would sail without them. That is all I have to say at the present time, except that if it was an inadvertence not to find out in each case just who grew these goods and what was the nationality of the individual, then I must admit I was remiss, but that question was never put up to me by anybody.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA VEGETABLE GROWERS
speechtext:
I would like to ask the
minister if he will be good enough to make every effort to have any further orders filled * by white producers if possible.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA VEGETABLE GROWERS
speechtext: We will surely give everybody, no matter what the colour of his skin is, an opportunity to supply these goods as long as the price and the quality are right.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY

speechtext:
The House resumed from Friday, March 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chevrier for the second reading of Bill No. 78 respecting the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company.
Mr. MA'NION:	Mr. Speaker, when the
time for the consideration of private bills came to an end on Friday night, I was dealing with the inadvisability of this House granting charters to any companies that, in a sense, are not bona fide. I pointed out that in the past there had been probably too much of a tendency to grant charters for various purposes to companies which were thus enabled to hold up the progress of the country. True, at times it is difficult to judge of the bona fides of those who apply for a charter, but I submit, Sir, that when the promoters do not exercise the powers which their charter supposedly intended them to take advantage of, then the granting of such a charter does harm to the country, in that the grantees are in a position to retard progress along certain lines on the plea that it might infringe upon their charter rights.
The present question has this merit, that it is not a party question, and every member can take his stand upon it without being accused of injecting party politics.
It is important to remember that the charter which under this bill it is now sought to extend was granted as far back as July 23, 1894, practically 33 years ago. Within two years of that date the work was to have been commenced and $50,000 expended, and in eight years it had to be finished or the charter would become null and void. Let me supplement that by reading section 44 of the original charter:

Georgian Bay Canal Company
If the construction of the canals hereby authorized, to be constructed, or some of them, is not commenced and fifty thousand dollars are not expended thereon within two years after the passing of this act, or if the said canals are not finished and put in operation within eight years after the passing of this act, then the powers granted by this act shall cease and be null and void as respects so much of the said canals and works hereby authorized as then remains uncompleted.
Instead of that charter being cancelled it has been renewed thirteen times, and this is the fourteenth application to the parliament of Canada for the same purpose. Practically no work has been done except perhaps some surveys in the way of general investigation; but so far as the construction of the canal goes absolutely nothing has taken place. I pointed out on Friday night that many of the original charter holders are dead, and looking over the list this morning I find such names as Sir Henry Egan, George Cox, Dennis Murphy, Sir James Grant and Mr. Bergeron, who at one time was a member of parliament. Many of these charter holders have died in the meantime, and still the charter is being renewed, from time to time, although nothing has been accomplished in the interests of the country. The rights of many of the original charter holders passed at one time into the hands of Sir Robert Perks, and according to a letter which I received this morning, and which I presume other members are in possession of, those rights have now gone to other parties.
The original rights were mainfy three. In the first place, they were empowered to build a canal nine feet deep, to use whatever water was necessary, to expropriate whatever lands they required, to build terminals, wharves, and so forth-the usual phraseology of such a charter. Secondly, they had the right to charge tolls on the use of the canal. In the third place-and this is the keynote of the whole matter-they had the right to produce, lease and supply hydraulic, electric or other kinds of power, and so on. The original purpose was to build a canal-the Georgian bay canal project which was much talked of in the old days-from the head of the lakes, whence I come, down along the Ottawa river. But I believe that to-day the real purpose behind the request for the renewal is to develop some of the million horse-power which exists on the river.
Let me deal for a moment or two with some of the rights given in the charter. In the first place, as regards the right of a private company to construct public waterways and to allow ships to use those waterways, for which use that private company

levies a toll, I believe the majority opinion, not only in Canada but throughout the world, is opposed to any permission being given to any such corporation to own the canals or waterways of a country and to make a profit therefrom. It is a bad principle to permit the private ownership of any of the waterways of the country, and that is one of the principal reasons I have to advance against the company building this canal, if indeed it had any intention of so doing. I submit that the government of Canada should own and control its own waterways; those waterways should not be given to any private corporation.
Then in regard to the power question:	I
will admit that in 1894 when the charter was originally granted the power possibilities in connection with the scheme were not thought of, as they are to-day. Power development had not at that time reached any considerable proportions, and there was not the same speculation regarding its future as there is to-day generally, particularly in this province. Indeed, I notice that the right to develop power was added to the charter merely as a subsidiary clause at the tail-end of one of the main provisions. Perhaps I had better read it. It is to be found in subsection (g) of section 8. They shall have the right to:
[DOT]-lay out and lease or otherwise dispose of waterlots, and use, sell, lease or otherwise dispose of water brought by or for the said canals or works but not requisite for the same, and produce, lease and supply, or otherwise dispose of hydraulic, electric and other kinds of power in connection with the works hereby authorized.
That, as I say, is really the tail-end of a paragraph. It is a subsidiary clause. And that more or less proves my contention that at the time the charter was given the real object in view was the building of a canal purely and simply, and not the development of power. The foregoing clause I have read, coming as it does as a sort of afterthought, shows beyond question that the power possibilities of the scheme were looked upon at the time as of minor importance. To-day, however, thirty-three years later, power development has become one of the supreme questions of the country. I made it my business this morning to ascertain what development there had been at Niagara since the granting of the charter; I wanted to find out if figures would not illustrate my contention better than any argument I could offer. I suspected that in 1894 there was little if any development of electrical power at Niagara falls, and so I rang up the officers of this government and asked them what development there was at the falls in that year. They

Georgian Bay Canal Company
replied, none. Yet to-day, thirty-three years later, there is being developed at Niagara, on the Canadian side, 1,000,000 horse-power, and on the American side 500,000 in round figures. So that there you have a total development of 1,500,000 horse-power of electrical energy at Niagara falls, and all this since the charter was originally granted. I need not offer further arguments to show how tremendously important power development has become to this country. The figures I have submitted amply demonstrate this.
One of the greatest factors in commercial progress in this or any other country to-day is the development of commercial electric power. In 1894 power could not be transmitted over any considerable distance. Since that time means have been devised whereby this can be done; power transmission over great distances is a matter of daily practice. That explains the rapid advance which power development has made. Take my own section of the country: Nipigon falls for very many years-I think I may safely say up to 1917-lay altogether idle. They were not developed at all. About the year 1917, however, Adam Beck decided to develop those falls, which have a potential hydro development of about 300,000 horse-power. As a result of the activities carried on there they have already developed 75,000 horse-power of that maximum, notwithstanding the fact that at the time the development there was proposed it was opposed by some people at the head of the lakes. That 75,000 horsepower is used to-day at Port Arthur and Fort William by the pulp and paper industry, and not only has it been a great blessing to that section of Canada, but the power development there will probably make for- this is not an exaggeration, for the facts substantiate the statement-one of the greatest pulp and paper industries in the world, if not, indeed, the greatest. That illustrates the importance of power in our country. The great province of Quebec to-day is a considerable industrial centre, and its importance in this respect is due very largely to the great waterways that exists there. Manitoba is in the same position; that province is gradually coming to the front in power development. The same is true in some measure of British Columbia and of the maritime provinces. A few months ago I happened to be at the opening of the Grand falls development in New Brunswick, and there I was struck with the possibilities of that enterprise, which is one of the great power developments in eastern Canada. I make these points only to emphasize the great importance of power to-day
It seems to me to be our duty in this House to guard these power rights for the people of the country.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
Is my hon. friend aware
that certain safe-guards already exist in the various supplementary acts relating to this scheme?

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: Of Ontario?

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
No, acts passed by the
Dominion parliament with regard to the various renewals of the charter.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
No, I am not aware of
that. My reading of the charter gives to the company very considerable rights with regard to the development of power on the Ottawa river. Of course, if ultimately it should turn out that they have no rights given them in the charter, I presume they would not object to having any supposed rights withdrawn. There would be no objection to their being confirmed in the right to build the canal, because I do not think they have any intention of building it anyway. My hon. friend the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Black) asks, how can the canal pay in competition with other waterways? I certainly do not believe the canal would pay without the power rights; it seems to me that the power development is what the company is after. It has been disputed that there is enough water to construct any large canals on the Ottawa river. I do not wish to be unfair; I am sure my hon. friend from Nipissing (Mr. Lapierre) has the facts ready to give the House, and I will admit that the government engineers who some years ago were asked to investigate the feasibility of the Georgian bay canal did state that they could develop a canal with a depth of twenty-two feet.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: That has been generally accepted all over the country.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
I am not disputing that in any way. I wish to read again section 44, because there is an item in this clause which, if this charter is renewed, gives this company a dangerous power. I will have to read the whole Clause to get the sense of it, but it is very short:
If the construction of the canals hereby authorized to be constructed, or some of them, is not commenced and fifty thousand dollars are not expended thereon within two years after the passing of this act, or if the said canals are not finished and put in operation within eight years after the passing of this act, then the powers granted by this act shall cease and be null and void as respects so much of the said canals and works hereby authorized as then remains uncompleted.
Georgian Bay Canal Company

As one of my hon. friends says that last sentence is the joker in this charter. That might give this company the right to build a great power scheme developing one million horse-power or even more on the Ottawa river; it would give them the right at the same time to start the construction of a canal within the eight years, or within the nine years, since I notice that in the charter now presented nine years has been made the limit, and if at the end of that time the government decided that this company was not going to carry out the building of that canal which was originally proposed in the charter, the government would be able to step in and say, "You apparently are not going to build a canal, and must stop any future development." But in that nine years this company might gobble up practically all the power which could be developed on the Ottawa river. Therefore that is another very strong reason, it seems to me, why we should hesitate to grant this charter as it now stands, and confer these powers upon this company.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
May I ask the hon.
gentleman a question? Is he avrare that there is a clause in that charter which allows the government to take over the work at any time?

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
Yes, and I am going to
read that clause later, but I am going to suggest that now is the time to take it over; nothing has been done in thirty-three years, and I think before anything is started is a good time to take it over.
Then there is another question which was brought up by Mr. Howard Ferguson, Premier of Ontario, with which no doubt he as a lawyer will be very much more familiar than I, because some of us in this House are not lawyers. That point has to do with the legal rights. Mr. Ferguson has pointed out, and it has been so stated by other lawyers, that at present it is an understood legal fact that the power rights are in the hands of the provinces and that the navigation rights are in the hands of the Dominion. I do not believe any one will dispute the latter statement, and on the other hand it can probably be proved before the courts that the power rights are in the hands of the provinces. If that is the case, we should make sure that that right remains with the provinces, and we should not take the risk of having a lawsuit on our hands by giving those rights to outsiders. In other words, this company might be given the right to build a canal, although I doubt very much if they will ever do so, but the provinces of Ontario and Quebec should retain their right 
to develop this power. When this question goes to committee, that point will be for the committee to decide.
I have a great deal of sympathy for my hon. friend from Nipissing and I also have sympathy for other hon. members who represent constituencies along the Ottawa river; in fact I have a little sympathy for myself, because the Ottawa and Georgian bay canal has been mooted in my part of the country for many years. But in reply to the arguments which I know the hon. member for Nipissing will later put on Hansard, I would say that he is really losing nothing for his constituency if this charter is not granted, because after all there is very little chance that this canal will ever be built even if this charter is granted; otherwise I might support him. Therefore he would simply be avoiding the danger of not having this canal developed until it is carried on later, probably by the government of our country.
Just to show the danger which such a charter suggests, I am going to quote for a moment from the Montreal Star of Thursday, March 3, 1927. In glancing over the news items in the Star I saw an advertisement which struck my eye. It was inserted by The Great Lakes and Atlantic Canal and Power Company, Limited1, and gave notice to the people of Canada that they are going to apply to the parliament of Canada at this session for a charter in which they ask for exactly the same rights on the St. Lawrence river between Montreal and Kingston as is asked for in the charter under consideration on the Ottawa river between Montreal and lake Nipissing. So if we grant the application of this Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company to go on with this work, there is no reason in the world why we should not grant the charter which is going to be requested by this other company. I have no idea who are the people represented by Mr. Harris, who signed this advertisement as secretary of the company, but without knowing who they are I say now that the proposition should be turned down just as I believe the charter now under consideration ought to be refused by this House.
I believe the St. Lawrence canal system will ultimately be developed; on that river to-day between Montreal and Kingston are some canals which are 260 feet long and which will allow the passage of a boat of 44 foot beam and 14 foot depth, but I believe that in the near future, using those words from a national standpoint rather than in their ordinary sense, the government will be able to begin the construction of canals which will permit larger boats to pass from the head of the lakes to Montreal, and possibly to cross

Georgian Bay Canal Company
the ocean. Even to-day there are boats which come across the Atlantic and proceed to the head of the lakes. As a boy, thirty years ago, I can remember a fairly large Norwegian boat, something over 240 feet in length, which came to the head of the lakes with a cargo from Norway and returned there with another cargo, and during navigation there are some small ships utilizing these canals on the St. Lawrence river. I believe that in the near future these canals will be enlarged in association with the development of the Welland canal, and that the grain of the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean) and of the farmers of the House and their friends, .instead of being carried to Port Colborne or Buffalo or Georgian bay ports, will go direct to Montreal where it will be transhipped to ocean going boats, and will be carried across the ocean with a saving to them of anywhere from five to ten cents a bushel. On the Welland canal we have already spent over $75,000,000, and ultimately our expenditure there will reach $110,000,000. Eighteen states of the union have declared themselves in favour of the development of the St. Lawrence river to a depth of 25 or 30 feet; these states have a population of 40,000,000 people, and are tributary to the great lakes. Herbert Hoover, Julius Barnes, the International Joint Commission and various other public bodies and public men in the United States have recently come out strongly in favour of the canalization of the St. Lawrence river. There is also on the St. Lawrence river some 4,000,000 horse power of potential electric energy to be developed, while on the Georgian Bay canal I believe there is something over 1,000,000 horse power. The estimated cost of developing the St. Lawrence canals, including the cost of the power scheme, is .-something like $252,000,000, and it has been recommended by the International Joint Commission that to this the cost of the Welland canal of which I spoke a moment ago should be added, and that the total should be divided between the two countries in proportion to the benefits received. In other words, if that were done and if the St. Lawrence canal scheme were carried through, the Dominion of Canada would not have very much to pay because of our vast expenditure in connection with the Welland canal. New York and Buffalo and some other centres which are opposing the canalization of the St. Lawrence will be to my mind ultimately defeated; they may delay the building of these canals but they cannot stop it. I submit that that canal would benefit not only the prairie provinces, by the lower rates on grain, but it would also benefit the city of Montreal.
1 do not believe, and in this I am supported by the opinions of shipping men, that ships would go across the ocean; they would transfer their cargoes at the port of Montreal or at some maritime port, and those cargoes would only undergo one transhipment instead of two or three, as is now the case.
To a certain extent the same argument would apply to the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian bay canal scheme if it were carried through. At the same time there is little chance of the canal feature of this project being proceeded with. I am pointing out merely the advantage, the ultimate advantage to Canada, of the other canals which I have no doubt will be built long before the Ottawa and Georgian bay canal and which will also put the maritime provinces in a more advantageous position in regard to the amount of coal which they could ship to the central parts of Canada. We imported last year from seventeen to eighteen million tons of coal, and of this amount some twelve million tons I think, of bituminous coal, most of which, or a large proportion of it,, was used in the province of Ontario. The maritime provinces cannot reach the province of Ontario at the present time with their coal because of the high cost of shipment from the port of Montreal west. But with the St. Lawrence canals deepened, as I think they will be deepened, the maritime provinces should be able to supply a large amount of the coal which is now being used in Ontario and other sections of Canada and which is being purchased from foreign countries.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not believe that this project should be given to a private corporation to develop; I believe it should be developed by this government. I believe that our waterways should remain in the hands of the government, and not be handed over to private corporations. In other words-and I have pretty nearly finished the argument I wish to make-I believe that both of these charters should be refused by this House; ultimately I believe they will be refused. I have noticed editorials in the Toronto Mail, Conservative; in the Toronto Globe, Liberal, and in the Ottawa Journal and Ottawa Citizen, of opposite sides of politics; and in the Montreal Gazette of this morning, all taking the same attitude, and all opposed to the granting of this charter. Mr. Ferguson, the Conservative Premier of Ontario, has come out and opposed it and he was supported in that attitude, as he is very rarely supported, by Mr. Raney. I believe that Mr. Sinclair will probably, although he has not announced himself so far as I know, take the same attitude as Mr. Ferguson and Mr. Raney. In other



Georgian Bay Canal Company
words there is almost a unanimity of desire to refuse to grant to these private people the right to develop electrical power and to develop the canal system on the Ottawa river. There will be no injustice,, it seems to me, in cancelling this right at the present time. I have already read to you section 44 of the company's charter. May I also read section 43, which is as follows:
Her Majesty

This was in the original charter and it is still in the charter.
*-her heirs and successors, may at any time assume the possession and property of the said canals and works, and of all the rights and privileges and advantages of the company, all of which shall after such assumption be vested in Her Majesty, her heirs and successors, on giving to the company one week's notice thereof and on paying to the company the value of the same, to be fixed by three arbitrators or the majority of them-
This is still a part of the charter which the company originally received. They had eight years originally, they have had in all thirty-three years to do something toward the development of this right, and they have done nothing. Therefore, I submit, there would be no injustice to them if you took from them any further rights they possess, giving them, of course, whatever compensation they might be entitled to by justice and by right.
I believe, Sir, that now is the best time to stop any further interference with the canal system, with the waterway system, of our country. I believe it is the duty of this parliament to take that step, and to refuse in the future to any company the right to take possession of our waterways. In the second place I believe it is the duty of this parliament to protect the waterways and electrical powers of our country for the benefit of the people of Canada.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
I wish to deal briefly with this very important measure. I think we are all indebted to the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley). for having, at this stage, brought to our attention the very far reaching character of the proposed measure, and while in ordinary cases a private bill does not meet with very much opposition or very much discussion at the present stage, nevertheless this bill, while appearing as a private bill is really a public bill, and is of such great importance that we are entitled to deal with it fully on the present occasion. My reason for discussing this bill is because of its relation to two of our problems, first, transportation, and secondly our industrial development as it is affected by hydro electric power. This fact
[Mr. Manion.l
emphasizes the importance of the measure. We have heard a great deal about our transportation system and our transportation difficulties, and much has been done in the last few years looking toward the solution of those difficulties, and also a great deal has been accomplished in the promotion of our industrial growth through the development of hydro electric power.
The senior member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) who has the bill in charge rather thought that its discussion at this stage was in the nature of opposition to the measure. But bearing in mind the importance of the bill* I do not think that is a fair contention. I think it might just as well be contended that the hon. member was perhaps endeavouring to rush the bill through committee as that we were endeavouring to obstruct it. What does this bill really propose to do? It relates to a charter that is thirty-three years old, to a charter granted in the year 1894, for the construction of a canal-or perhaps more correctly speaking a series of canals-on the Ottawa river. That charter, as has been said, has been renewed thirteen times. One would have thought that the company had had ample time to go ahead and undertake this work if it ever intended to do so. This great lapse of time should arrest and command the attention of the House. It makes it our duty to look into the situation now and compare it to the situation that existed thirty-three years ago. The situation, as has already been pointed out, is an altogether different one. We must look upon the matter as conditions exist to-day rather than as they existed thirty-three years ago.
A careful reading of the charter makes it perfectly plain that the main object was the construction of this canal or series of canals, and that the development of hydraulic or electric power was only incidental to the main undertaking. The charter provided that the company that constructed the canal should have the right to charge toll. Now I think it is absolutely sound to contend that all waterways, all canals of this character, should be built, owned and operated by the Dominion itself. That is the policy which we have been following in Canada with such success, and in pursuance of which we have made such enormous expenditures of money. The construction of the canal at an earlier period would have been much more feasible than at the present time except for the power question. The cost of construction thirty-three years ago and down until the time of the war would have been much less than it is now. We must assume that the companv

Georgian Bay Canal Company
have made reasonable efforts to carry out the privileges, the opportunities, which this charter has granted them. Yet in this long period of thirty-three years they have not been able to finance the matter, to construct the canal, nor to do anything practical to show that the proposition is one that can be carried out.
As I have said, conditions have changed entirely and perhaps there has been no greater change than in connection with our canals. 'Since this charter has been granted we have enlarged the Soo canal; we have enlarged the St. Lawrence canal; we have undertaken the construction of the Welland canal, and surely all this work that has been carried out and that is in progress must have an effect upon the transportation question and upon the route which the grain will take. All these must operate to the detriment and disadvantage of the proposed Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian bay canal.
Before we engage in any further canal construction we should see how these improvements will work out and what effect they will have upon the transportation of our grain and commerce generally. We also have the fact that the Panama canal has been constructed and is exercising a considerable influence upon the movement of grain. The Hudson bay railway is under construction, and if this route is of any value at all, if it is practicable, it will have an effect and will divert traffic which might in the beginning have been expected to find its way by this proposed canal.
While there has been this very striking change in the canal situation, there has been an equally striking and important change in connection with the power situation. In the period of thirty-three years the whole hydroelectric system of Ontario and of the adjoining province of Quebec has grown up and has assumed an influence and place, the importance of which we can scarcely over-estimate, in the industrial development of those two provinces. We must consider this proposition in the light of this feature and if this charter is renewed, this company, while acquiring the right to construct the canal and to levy tolls as against free canals-and this in itself appears to be an unsound proposition-will have in its control the development of 1,000,000 or 1,125,000 horse-power. Not only Ontario and Quebec, but the whole Dominion of Canada is vitally interested in this proposition. I cannot think of anything that touches our life at more vital points than the development of hydro-electric power. It has much to do with our industrial development; it has a great deal to do with transportation on 3264ft-604
our railway systems; it will have much to do in solving our immigration problem, and is therefore one of the most important features of our industrial life to-day. Is it right or proper that by a side wind, as it were, we should hand over to this company, when such was not in contemplation in the original transaction, the control, the disposition of 1,000,000 horse-power? Such a proposition is so unreasonable, so contradictory to the public welfare, that it ought not to be entertained for a moment.
When we are asked to give this company a fourteenth renewal of its charter, surely the promoters of this bill must make out a very clear case. They must be compelled to show that it is in the public interest that this renewal should be granted at this time. Let us see what the effect of the renewal will be apart from what I have already stated. Supposing the company does nothing as it has done nothing for thirty-three years, the effect of inaction will foe to tie up this 1,000,000 horse-power for eight or ten years longer and also to tie up the development of the canal system on this river. This surely was not contemplated and it cannot be favourably contemplated at the present time.
The next question which arises is this: Have we any jurisdiction to grant to this company the rights for which they are asking? It is admitted, of course, that this parliament is supreme in the matter of navigation; but we have had several decisions with respect to the rights of the provinces to surplus waters, the lands under the waters and the riparian rights, and I think I am safe in saying that there is at least very grave doubt whether the Dominion of Canada has any right to grant to a company the use of surplus waters or the right to develop hydro-electric power. The rights of the two provinces interested must be recognized. We should not do anything that will delay the possibility of their carrying out legitimate developments along these lines. We should not, with our eyes open as it were, do anything that will lead to conflict, to litigation, with these provinces, and surely if this charter is renewed we may expect that to be the result. Ontario is hungering for the development of hydroelectric power, and the two sources from which we are looking for this development in eastern Ontario are the Ottawa river and the St. Lawrence river. An obstacle has been placed in the way of development on the Ottawa river by the action of this parliament in granting this charter, and we think the time has now come when that obstacle can be removed, when at least it should not be continued, and

Georgian Bay Canal Company
when Ontario and Quebec, each being equally interested in this power, should be free to go ahead and make this development.
On the St. Lawrence river there are complications of a different character, but action again on the part of this government is necessary before we can get any relief. Let me as a representative of one of the constituencies of eastern Ontario urge this government to take every action possible for the early removal of these obstacles and for the cooperation which is necessary with the provinces for the development of hydro-electric power on these two streams. Let me suggest also to the government that perhaps this is an opportune time to clean up the Chicago water steal. Our friends in the United States are very anxious to enter into some arrangement for the development of hydro-electric power on the St. Lawrence, and it would be only fair and right to say to them that before we will enter into an agreement on this question we must have a complete clean-up and settlement in connection with the Chicago water steal.
This is not a party question and should not be. It is not a question of one or two provinces against the rest of the Dominion, but a matter in which we are all interested and for which we wish to find the best possible solution in the public interest. In support of my contention, I refer to two editorials in the Toronto Globe, the first appearing on March 2, 1927, from which I will quote a couple of paragraphs. The article is headed The Georgian Bay Canal, and reads:
This is the measure which would have been endorsed in principle last week had it not been for the interference of Sir George Perley. It will come before the House again, and it will bear watching. The existence of this charter and of the vague hope that the canal will be built prejudices discussion of St. Lawrence development plans. If the canal were constructed and operated under the charter, a system of toll charges would be permitted, while tolls on all other canals in Canada have been abolished. Most serious of all, however, would be the handicap under which the development of negotiations of hydro would be placed along the route involved.
In the public interest Parliament can hardly take this charter seriously any longer. The company has not even filed with the government working plans which have met with approval. Thirty-three years has been a long enough time to toy with a valuable public franchise.
Then, in the same paper, a very able editoral headed The Bill Should be Killed deals with the matter more exhaustively, and I quote from that editorial, as follows:
When the charter was granted in 1894 the advantages of public ownership were not fully

understood. Conditions are different to-day. The importance of water-power is appreciated. The people of the Ottawa valley and of all the territory contiguous to these rivers will profit immeasurably if they are given the full benefit of the "white coal" which now awaits development in that part of the country. If this power is permitted to become the property of private interests they will pay dearly for its use, while under public ownership they will have it in perpetuity at cost. It is their duty, no less than that of tne rest of the province, to see that this advantage is retained.
The building of a canal and the exploitation of power are two distinct matters. If the company wants to build a canal, this should not confuse the more immediate and more important question of power. It would be serious enough to give a private corporation the right to own and control what will be in time, no doubt, an important navigation channel, but to alienate from the public 1,000,000 or more horse-power of current for the purpose of public exploitation and to enter into competition with public ownership is something which this Province cannot tolerate.
So that we have the two objections. To sum it up, we have the objection that the canal should not be constructed by a company with the right to charge tolls, and the other objection that the immense power possibilities should not be handed over to any private company. I wish to make a few suggestions in connection with this matter, which I hope will commend themselves to the House. I submit that we should decline to renew this charter, and that the government should pronounce against any such renewal. In the second place, I think we should divorce- perhaps that is a good term-the canal proposition from the power proposition. We grant many divorces in this parliament and I think such a divorce would be more deserving than many that we do grant The construction of the canal should be undertaken as a public work at the public cost, and the power proposition should be developed by the two provinces and the Dominion jointly. The share of the power to which the province of Ontario is entitled going to the Hydro-Electric Power Commission, and the share which the province of Quebec is entitled to going as that province may direct. Let us construct the canal as a public work, and let us divide the power. At present it would appear that the three jurisdictions have, as it were, a blocking right in connection with this development. This government may, in its jurisdiction with respect to navigation, obstruct the provinces from undertaking development, and the provinces may also obstruct the Dominion, a right which they undoubtedly have, which will prove very embarrassing. So that it seems to me that the Dominion and the two prov-

Georgian Bay Canal Company
inces should get together, that they should decide not to renew this charter, that they should agree upon a plan for the development of power that will not interfere with navigation, and if, in connection with the development of power, some portion of the cost should be paid for improvement in navigation, then a contribution in this direction should be made. All three, the Dominion, the province of Ontario, and the province of Quebec are equally interested on behalf of the .public and in the public interest, and it should not be hard for the three authorities to get together and arrive at some solution which would be fair to these people who hold the charter. They have held this charter for thirty-three years. It has been renewed, and I would make them a reasonable and fair compensation for any work they have undertaken, as provided in the charter itself.

speechtext: I hope they will spend a lot more money investigating before they hand this charter over to any private company again. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it had not been my intention to speak at any length on this occasion, but as there has been considerable discussion and as the subject matter of this bill means much to
us in northern Ontario, for on the construction of the proposed canal depends our future industrial development, and we have waited patiently for it for 30 years, I am going to ask the indulgence of the House while I treat this subject from the standpoint of the people in northern Ontario.
As has been repeatedly said, this project has been before the House for at least 33 years, and for 14 years its promoters have secured renewals of their charter. In 1921 and again in 1924 renewals were granted without any objection. In northern Ontario we do not look upon this as merely a power project. To us it is a project of national importance, for not only is the province of Ontario interested in its realization, but it is of vital interest to the farmers of the prairie provinces and to the coal miners in Nova Scotia. So great is the interest in northern Ontario and so consistently have the people there advocated the construction of this canal, that I propose to read a few telegrams that I have received from different parts of the province:

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
I will come to that in
a moment. We regard the question as one of transportation. Northern Ontario has become one of the largest wealth producing sections of that province. As so ably demonstrated by my hon. friend from Fort William a few days ago, northern Ontario is now one of the largest and most promising mining fields in the world. We have produced in that district within the last twenty-five years over nine hundred million dollars' worth of minerals. In the section in which I live we have produced over 85 per cent of the world's nickel, while throughout the north country, in all that great pre-Cambrian shield which blankets the whole of northern Ontario, there exists one of the greatest stores of * Mother Nature's wealth, of which we have scratched only 5 per cent. This part of Canada has contributed more during the last fifteen years to the industrial development of older Ontario, to the development of the industrial centres of the province, to the trade of Toronto and many other cities, than any other factor in the commercial life of the province. To-day that section of the country, producing immense wealth, finds itself on the eve of seeing concluded a project which will mean a greater development than it has ever known. It means the canalization of the Ottawa river which will link us up with the great lakes and with the lower ports of the St. Lawrence. By the plans which were deposited with the government a few years ago, construction will take place a little above the confluence of the Mattawa and the Ottawa rivers which will render the great lakes navigable right into the mining country of Ontario, bringing Haileybury, New Liskeard and Ville-Marie, as seaports, into direct communication with the various ports of Canada.
This is the great scheme that has agitated northern Ontario for the last twenty-five years and it is to-day so near realization that the people are anxious to see it carried to a successful conclusion. What is the opposition to this scheme? We heard no opposition to the construction of the Georgian bay ship canal until there was a move to control the Carillon water-power. Now we find considerable opposition developing. On the upper Ottawa the agents and engineers of the International Paper Company have men investigating the great water-powers, and in a few days we shall see two or three great dams built on the upper waters of the Ottawa which will actually control 1,000,000 horsepower. This will come into the possession of a private corporation, as happened on the Gatineau. We in Ontario who have waited for the development of the northern country know that if we are to have a Georgian bay ship canal we must secure it through the means of power development. It must be carried by power, and any other scheme projected or suggested will not meet the requirements of the northern section of that province nor give the transportation facilities to which that part of the Dominion is entitled.
What are the promises of the company on which we base our hopes for an early construction of the canal? I have before me a part of the brief which has been discussed. We know very well that it became very difficult after the close of the war to obtain cheap money. As was stated by the hon. member for Argenteuil, Sir Robert Perks came to this House year after year, for many years, and attempted to obtain the assistance necessary to carry out a national undertaking of this importance. But to-day in view of this im-

Georgian Bay Canal Company
provement and in view of the increased value of water-power, the holders of this charter find that if they are permitted to have the charter extended for two years more they can give northern Ontario these transportation facilities which have long been promised. Here is what they propose to do. Upmi the granting of this charter they will immediately start the construction of that section of the canal from Montreal to Ottawa. This will take about three years and will produce 219,000 horse-power at Carillon and 4,100 horsepower at Ste. Anne's. This would give continuous navigation as far up the river as the city of Ottawa, and would make Ottawa a port; it would complete 120 miles out of a total of 440 miles, or 27 per cent of the whole project; the cost will be about $55,000,000, all of which will be new money spent in Canada and which constitutes roughly 20 per cent of the total cost of the project. Completion of this section will extend continuous navigation up the Ottawa river from salt water to above AmprioV. The next section, section 2, will take two years to complete; it will produce 158,000 horse-power, will be 54 miles in length or about 12 per cent of the total mileage and will cost about $40,000,000, or roughly 14 per cent of the total cost.

speechtext: What is the hon. member referring to?

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
This is the brief of the charter company. These details can all be discussed in committee. At the end of five years a total of 174 miles will have been constructed at a cost of $95,000,000, or 24 per cent of the complete project in mileage and 34 per cent in money. Now, Mr. Speaker, we in northern Ontario who have waited patiently all these years feel that under the circumstances this government will be perfectly justified in extending this charter for another two or three years; we have already waited 30 years, during which no objections have been made to this power proposition. The situation as it is to-day would mean that the granting of separate power rights on the upper Ottawa river would remove the possibility of a canal for all time, and that accounts in a very large measure for the numerous telegrams I have received and for the anxiety which exists in the north country over this enterprise. According to the plans which are now on deposit with the government, an expenditure of $282,000,000 within the next ten years is called for, and under this charter the provincial rights are reserved. But we find ourselves in this position, that whilst the power development will be available for the government of Ontario, we have in the prov-	: t i
ince of Quebec a government which is opposed to government ownership, which means that this water-power development will eventually come into the hands of one company, creating another great power monopoly on the Ottawa river and leaving the owners of remaining timber limits at the mercy of this corporation. That is what we in northern Ontario envisage in this situation.
The feasibility of the canal has long been conceded, and the plans have been before this government for a number of years. The engineering difficulties which were numerous in the early days of survey have entirely disappeared, and there is no longer any fear that these difficulties will be encountered. Furthermore, I would warn my friends from Montreal that the scheme which no doubt the large power corporations are going to put into effect on the waters of the upper Ottawa river will make a tremendous difference in the water levels of the St. Lawrence river. All engineers will tell you that under the modem system of constructing dams, where large areas of low lying lands are flooded and large bodies of water are exposed to evaporation, you will have a continual reduction in the water level, and that is what will happen if the waters of the upper Ottawa are dammed in order to create large units of electrical power. On the other hand, if you allow this canal scheme to be carried on along the lines called for by the plans, in order to maintain navigation it becomes necessary that you retain the water level at 24 feet. The plans as they exist to-day call for a canal 24 feet deep from the Georgian bay to Montreal, capable of accommodating the largest ships sailing the great lakes. It will be the most economical route for the shipment of grain, and this is a question which has been discussed before. All of our Progressive friends are familiar with the transportation costs on grain, but we know that once this canal is opened there will be a very great diversion of the grain now carried by the way of Buffalo.; the route will be shorter by several hundred miles; it will be entirely within Canadian territory and absolutely under the control of the Dominion government, and grain will be carried for at least three cents a bushel less than it is carried to-day.
Now let us consider the situation in northern Ontario, where we use tremendous quantities of coal in our mines. There is a continuous demand for coal in northern Ontario, because most of our ores have to be treated. We are at present importing into the town of North Bay alone over 980,009

Georgian Bay Canal Company
tons of bituminous coal and the saving on that coal alone if it were transported by water would be over $1,250,000. Just think for a .moment what it means to that part of Ontario if the French river development is completed; North Bay, now a city with a population of 15,000, would be a centre of water navigation. To-day North Bay is the front door of this great northern country; it is gradually becoming a great commercial centre but until we have more power in order to attract industries, we must for a number of years remain at a standstill. We have an excellent proof of that in the fact that a few years ago the International Nickel Company, for want of electric power, was forced to go to Port Colbome and erect its smelters there. A few years ago also the British American Nickel Company, which has spent over $25,000,000 in the development of the Murray mine at Sudbury, was compelled to erect its refineries at a point within a few miles of Ottawa, where it could get large quantities of hydraulic and electric power at a very low figure. Now, Sir, within the last few years, near one of the largest nickel deposits in the world, a discovery has been made of lead and. zinc and we are told to-day -in fact I have the figures here-by those interested in the enterprise that they have already blocked out 43,000,000 tons of these valuable minerals, possessing a value of $22 a ton. Here we are the centre of a mining industry producing some of the richest ores known to mineral science-which attract high salaried men of the most expert class, which brings skilled metallurgists and engineers who are the most advanced in their knowledge of the development of our ores-and yet we find these ores being carried miles away from where they are mined, creating new centres of industry elsewhere because we have not the water-power or electric power with which to treat them. That is the situation which exists in our northern country to-day. We up there are in favour of this project as it stands because we look upon it as our only salvation, if we are ever to establish industries in addition to those of farming and mining. At the present moment in the district of Sudbury we have developed all the available water-power, amounting to some 37,500 horsepower, which is being used by the nickel industry and by the pulp and paper industry, and we have practically exhausted all the electric power procurable. But what we lack can be made up by the construction of the Georgian bay ship canal. It would also help to solve our coal problem. Ships on the great lakes could carry grain to the maritime provinces, and bring back Nova Scotia coal at a rate that would make its transportation possible, and thus help a great deal to develop our fuel problem.
I have not entered into a discussion of the legal phase of the question, I leave that to those who are better posted on that aspect of the matter than I am. But I want to make it clear to hon. gentlemen that the people of northern Ontario, the red-blooded pioneers who have helped to develop that northern country, have their eyes focused on this question. This is a great national undertaking which has been promised to us by each succeeding government. I remember hearing Sir Wilfrid Laurier state in the city of Montreal many years ago, that when once the Grand Trunk Pacific had been completed the next great national undertaking upon which this country would have to embark would be the construction of the Georgian bay ship canal. Nothing has transpired, except perhaps the desire of certain groups to secure possession of these water-powers, which should be allowed to interfere with the granting of this charter and the undertaking and completion of a great national project.
