speechtext:
The hon. member for
Kingston. I wish to state out of courtesy to the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), that I have before me a long list of speakers and that I am following the old rule of alternating between the speakers of different parties or groups in the House.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
At the outset let me assure the last speaker, the good people of northern Ontario, and all others who are interested in the Georgian bay canal, that I for one have no objection to its construction. So far as I am concerned I am in great sympathy with all my hon. friend has said concerning neiw or northern Ontario. We all recognise the vast resources of that great country, and we in the older parts of the province would be the last people in the world to place any obstacle in the way of its development.
One would be very foolish at this stage of our civilization to deny the importance of canalization, or to deny that water-borne transportation is not the cheapest means of transportation at the present day. All the essential factors have demonstrated the truth of that proposition. Therefore I am interested in schemes of canalization in this country, but I am also interested in seeing that the development shall proceed along proper lines.

Georgian Bay Canal Company
In regard to the present scheme, I wish to say that there are three principal questions to be discussed: first, the attitude of the government or the state towards canalization: second, the importance of the power factor: third, the legal aspect of the case. The first and very important question, that of the attitude of the government towards the canalization of any or all sections of the country is an interesting one. History has proven that very rarely has any country handed over to private corporations or private companies the development of its canal system. Canal systems existed in the days of the Pharaohs and even before that time. Ever since 7000 B.C. we have evidence of the existence of canal systems. There was the canal of Babylon, built about 1700 B.C. and renewed by Nebuchadnezzar in 600 B.C. The present Suez canal had1 a predecessor which lasted from 600 B.C. down to 760 A.D The Romans built canals and I want to point out the fact that all ancient systems of canals were state built and state maintained. Coming down now to European systems we find that the Dutch built the great Amsterdam canal, in fact the whole of Holland is a network of canals comprising some 2,408 miles. These canals are all built and maintained by the state and no tolls are collected. Belgium, perhaps, has reached the highest state of perfection in canal development. She has seven or eight very important canals with a total length of 1,346 miles. All these canals are state owned and state maintained and are free of tolls. France has 3,030 miles of canals of which 2,860 are state owned and free of all tolls. In fact no tolls have been collected in that country since 1888. Germany has had a canal system since 1700. She has connected all her commercially stategic points by canals, but the fact is important that they have been built by the state and1 are free of tolls to the public. It is well known that German industrial life owes its great importance and development to the splendid system of canalization that exists in that country, and yet, not satisfied with that, Germany has developed a splendid system of canals for purely military purposes.
Russia under Peter the Great started her canal system connecting St. Petersburg with the Caspian sea, with the Artie sea, and in all cases these canals are state-owned, state-maintained and free from tolls. Austria-Hungary had 1,700 miles of a state-owned canal system. Going through this historical section of canal development we come to Great Britain and we find she is the only country with privately-owned canals. The railways own one-third of her canal systems. There is this significant

fact that Great Britain was not so intensely interested as other countries were in building canals. The Thames and the Severn have a great watershed and this supply of water gave these rivers freer means of navigation than we find in other countries. As a matter of fact canals built by Great Britain have not done so much towards developing industrial life as have canals in ' other countries. The greatest canal in Great Britain is the Manchester ship canal and it really had its beginning in a privately-owned canal. Its beginning was due to the fact that the Duke of Bridgewater wanted to connect his collieries with Manchester, and from that beginning the local people became interested in building a ship canal with the idea of connecting Manchester with the coast, and avoiding the obstructions at Liverpool, dues and so on. It was due more to the interest of those local people, large interests around Manchester, Salford and other big cities in that district, that this canal has been the success it has. But the mere fact that many of these canals were undertaken by private companies is no argument for privately-owned canals, the private interests were driven to construct them, but many fell into the possession of the railway companies who put on such high tolls that the canal development and water transportation could not be made use of, and that the railroads received a greater amount of transportation than the canals, offsets any argument in this case in favour of the construction of canals by privately-owned companies.
This brings us from Europe to the United States, and their experience is very interesting. Shortly after the war of the American Revolution there arose a movement to connect New' York with the great lakes. That began when twyo private companies were formed, one to build a canal to connect with lake Champlain and the other to build a canal to connect with lake Erie. The company that was to build a canal to connect with lake Champlain failed. The other company built about six miles of internal canals and that was as far as it went until a commission, with Governor Clinton at its head, was appointed by the state of New York. This commission kept at work for many years until finally the Erie canal was built from Buffalo to New York. We are told that on the opening of that canal a great celebration was held over the arrival at New York of the first boat from Buffalo. A famous picture called the Marriage of Waters has been painted of that event. Two bottles of water were taken from lake Erie and one was emptied into the

Georgian Bay Canal Company
Atlantic at Sandy Hook. At that celebration some very enthusiastic United States citizen conceived the idea of collecting water from rivers and navigable streams all over the world and these were also brought there and emptied. What I want to point out in connection with this historical section is the fact that in nearly all these cases the canals were built by the state, state-owned, state-maintained and free from tolls. So far as I know and can read, the only privately-owned ones in America have been failures. The Delaware and Hudson Company in the early days built a canal 108 miles long, but that canal has gone into the scrap heap. Those canals that have remained, that have been in any way a success, have been state-owned, state- maintained and free from tolls.
Let us judge the application for this charter by that historical fact. This is a company which wants to build a canal which, if built, will no doubt be of great benefit to this country, will help to develop it, will help in transportation in every way; but this company is going back to the old system of tolls, and1 T can assure the House that this system, in competition with railway transportation, will be a failure just as the canals about Liverpool have been.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: Does the hon. member know of any canal in the United States, England, Belgium or Germany that was developing power at the same time?

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
I do not know. I
have divided my remarks into three subjects and I am coming to the subject of power. Canalization is the important factor. If canalization is not an important factor, then power is the only factor and I will deal with that as my second subject. I want to point out that if this canal is built to be used for transportation purposes and tolls are charged, it will be a failure.
I come to the second point which is that of power. I have been asked: Do I know of any canal that has been built combining power development with water transportation? I say no and I do not know where there ever was such a situation as will arise in this case. I do not think the power development on this Georgian bay canal will enable the canal to be completed. It was pointed out in this House to-day that the scheme in the past was a failure because government guarantees were not behind it. What is behind this is the power scheme, the question of deriving revenue from the power development, and before I am through with this second section I want to show that this will also hardly be possible.
Coming to the second factor in the granting of this charter, the development of power: .This is a very pertinent question to the province of Ontario. It affects the people and the municipalities of Ontario in a very peculiar way. About the year 1900 the people of Ontario were seized with the great possibilities of the development of their industrial life. We had, as the last speaker said, great natural resources in mining, forestry and agriculture, but the one drawback to the development of these was the fuel situation. We felt that we were prevented from attaining our ideal through want of fuel. Looking for a solution of this difficulty, the citizens in various parts of the provinces began to study the possibilities of power on our many rivers, principally on the Niagara river. The possible replacement of power for fuel which we had to bring into this country appealed very strongly to the citizens of Toronto. I am in perfect accord with the last speaker that if by this means we can bring 'in fuel, then we are all willing to assist in the best possible way to supply it. From 1900 events quickly followed in the development of the scheme of power to replace fuel. In 1900 a committee of the Toronto board of trade made a report on the subject of hydro-electric power from the Niagara river. The large towns and cities, even the rural municipalities, quickly became imbued with the desire to reach some solution of the question and to bring about an increase in power. The matter became the subject of meetings, the subject of press comments and reference on the hustings, but no means of action was possible. No matter how much these citizens of Ontario would talk on this question, or how much it was discussed in the public press, there was no way of taking action to institute such a scheme, until in 1903 .the legislature of Ontario passed an act providing means for 'the appointment of a commission to interest itself in the scheme and to harmonize the different ideas of the municipalities. The plan was to investigate the question of supply and distribution of hydroelectric power, and such municipalities as desired could form themselves into groups and take the matter up. The first commission was formed by the municipalities of Toronto, London, Brantford, Stratford, Woodstock, Ingersoll and Guelph, known as the Ontario Power Commission. Its report gave data on the resources of power from coal, gas, oil and water. In 1906 this report was published, but before the information it contained became very generally known (throughout the province, action had already been taken, because in that same year, 1906, the legislature of Ontario

Georgian Bay Canal Company
passed an act for the creation of the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario. At first this commission was to receive appeals and requests from the different municipalities, but it soon became no longer a board of harmony. The demand became so great that it became a board of go-getters of power of Ontario. It became a central body representative of the municipality and acting on their behalf. In 1908 this commission made its first purchase of power-100,000 horsepower-from the Ontario Power Company of Niagara. The commission then began its first active work in the transmission of this power, and I would like now to refer to the efforts of the commission, first to solve the fuel problem, second to make available a supply of power, and third to transmit that power to the people of Ontario.
In 1910 the company started to distribute this power, having completed its transmission line, and still the demand grew. In 1915 that 100,000 horse-power was exhausted. In 1915 and 1916 it had to purchase an additional supply of 50,000 horse-power from the Ontario Power Company, and 25,000 horse-power from the Toronto Power Company. A new stage in its growth was now reached, when the supply from the privately owned companies failed or became exhausted. In 1917 the hydro-electric commission had to purchase the Ontario Power company, and in 1919 it increased the output from 160,000 horse-power to 200,000 horse-power. In 1920 the commission purchased the Toronto Power Company with its output of 125,000 horse-power. And so, with lightning speed, this commission has gone on from growth to growth, and almost every morning, in the words of a famous British statesman, one had to inquire what new development had taken place. Its last and greatest development, when all power from privately owned companies and from all possible rivers which were open to them were exhausted, was the Queenston-Chippawa proposition, which has developed 600,000 horse-power on the Niagara river. This was a scheme practically of turning a river and making it run in the opposite direction; because our allowance- of power on t'he Niagara was exhausted. In addition to this, the commission has generated power on the Severn, at Wasdell's and the Eugenia falls and practically surrounded two-thirds of this province with its power scheme. In addition to that, they have taken all the power they could gather from privately owned plants on the Ottawa, the Rideau, in the Muskoka district, the St. Lawrence, and the Nipissing, and distributed it to the municipalities.

I now wish to give a few figures to further show the usefulness and service of this great commission. In 1910 the commission distributed 1,000 horse-power to a number of municipalities in Ontario. In 1914 they had supplied 77,000 horse-power, in 1920, 356,000 horse-power, and in 1923, 050,000 horse-power, and to-day it supplies to the people of Ontario, 900,000 horse-power. The demand has come from factories, from farms, Lor lighting for the streets, for the roadways, from all parts and all sections of this country. The transmission line of this commission extends over 3,000 miles. The distribution of power varies from one mile to 250 miles, the greatest distance of distribution which is accomplished by the transmission of Niagara power to the city of Windsor. The commission is under contract to develop power at cost to the municipalities, which in turn distribute to its citizens at cost. In this way the hydroelectric commission is supplying 226 municipalities in the province of Ontario. The total assets of the commission amout to 1250,000,000, and it supplies a population of 1,000,000. In the face of these facts, is there any reason for the granting of a charter to a private company for the development of power on the Georgian bay canal? My argument is this:	That the citizens of Ontario have taken upon themselves the development of this great hydro-electric power, its assets are all owned by the municipalities and the province of Ontario; that it was undertaken at a time when there was a great need, a great hunger for power in this province; that at this very day that hunger has not been satisfied by any means, and that the commission is ready to develop on the Ottawa, on the St. Lawrence or on any other river where power is available if it is not checked and obstructed by legislation of this kind. Undoubtedly, by extending this charter the Dominion government would be doing a grave injustice to the people of Ontario and their public-owned hydro-electric undertaking.
The province of Ontario or the province of Quebec must supply the demand for power which would be available but for this charter, and consequently by renewing it we are virtually enabling a private company to enter into competition with or obstruct a people-owned scheme of hydro-electric power. It has been suggested to-day that Ontario and Quebec could not cooperate in this matter because while Ontario has developed a public-owned power system, the sister province has encouraged privately-owned projects for the generation of power. I cannot see that this of itself is any serious objection. I have no doubt that the two provinces can reach a

Georgian Bay Canal Company
caramon, agreement for the development of the power on the Ottawa river. Certainly there is not the slightest excuse for leaving this development in the hands of a private company that in the course of 33 years has made no attempt to cater to the transportation needs of the people of Ontario and Quebec. Had this company made any effort to serve the people along this line there might be some reason for renewing the 'charter. The ostensible purpose of the charter is to 'build a canal, but nothing having been done in this direction since the granting of the charter, it is not unreasonable to assume that the promoters of the bill are more concerned now with the power features of the project. Once the charter is renewed they will be placed in a position to compete with a publidly-owned system in which the people of Ontario have invested two hundred and fifty million dollars, and which is serving over a million of the population of the province with lig'ht and power. Obviously it would be most unfair to submit that undertaking to such obstruction.
I have tried to show that canal development of the world has been altogether along the lines of state ownership. This of itself is a further argument against granting a renewal of the charter rights of the company to construct a canal, which undoubtedly would in any event be merely incidental to the development of power along the course of the canal, and, as I have already said, this would be grossly unfair to the Hydro Electric Commission of Ontario, which is ready and willing to still further serve the needs of the people in the way of power and light. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I submit that it would be a great mistake to put that publicly-owned scheme in competition with a private company by granting a renewal of this charter.
I think it will be generally agreed that in the past we have made mistakes in our transportation undertakings, 'both water and rail, and in the development of our harbours and rivers. I think the day is at hand when the government should appoint a permanent board of engineers to survey the whole dominion and report from time to time as to what harbours and rivers should be developed, and what canals should be built in the public interest. In a word, we should lay down a definite policy in dealing with our canals, railways, harbours and rivers, so that a system economical and efficient might be built up. We all know that the United States made many mistakes in canal building. I need only refer to one with which we are all more or less familiar-the Erie canal. On its completion there came demands for lateral and other canals, many of which were not needed, and,
although they were undertaken, most of them became failures. We do not want to repeat our neighbour's mistakes. In support of my proposal that the government' should appoint a board of engineers to deal with our canal and cognate problems, I may point to the board constituted by the government to report on the feasibility of the deepening of the St. Lawrence river. The board that I suggest the government should appoint could deal with our system of canals, and incidentally they could investigate the water-powers available in connection with any canalization projects, and report their findings to the government, which in turn, of course, would place them on the table of the House for the information of members.
I think we are at a stage of our national development that would warrant perhaps further canalization, but lest we repeat our Welland canal mistake, I think we should be guided by expert advice. I should like to have some report from a strong board of engineers on the feasibility this canal and whether within say, three, six or nine years it will be constructed and in operation. I know no other country except China that has waited so long for a canal. China started a canal to connect her capital with the coast, but it was not completed for 600' years. If we are to trust to the company which is asking for a renewal of this charter, I fear even the Chinese record will be broken. Before the charter is renewed the government should come to the House and say, "We are satisfied and will take the responsibility of recommending its renewal."
Not being a lawyer, I shall not deal with the legal question, but the government must assume the responsibility of assuring this House that they are ready to meet the case of the province of Ontario. Very strong statements have been made by Premier Ferguson that provincial power rights in the Ottawa river will be upheld in the courts. Therefore, hon. members of this House who come from all over the dominion look to the government for advice. The government should be our advisers as to how we should vote-or at least, they should give us some advice.

speechtext:
I
trust the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) will not charge me with indulging in reprehensible tactics if I venture to discuss the subject before the House. I am a comparatively new member and I still have a great deal to learn with respect to matters of rule and procedure, but it seems to me a somewhat unusual situation to have such an important measure as this introduced into this House, a measure involving so many varied interests, without receiving any information from the sponsor of the bill as to what its purpose is. I had hoped when the bill was introduced by the senior hon. member for Ottawa that we might have -been given some information as to what is contained in the measure itself. Personally, not being a member of the legal profession, I find it very difficult indeed to fathom the provisions of the bill as presented to the House. It has been contended by those in favour of the bill-as a matter of fact, so far, only one hon. member has spoken in support of it- that if it passes the House the people of northern Ontario will have the canal built for them forthwith. I presume that if I had been a member of this House thirty years ago, listening to the original promoters of this undertaking, I should have heard them say exactly the same thing as was said this afternoon by the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Lapierre). That is always the view put forward in this House -by promoters seeking charters, and I for one ami opposed to this parliament giving charters of this kind, particularly where so much is involved as is the case in the bill now before us. It is almost a third of a century since the charter was originally granted, and on thirteen occasions it has been renewed. I cannot therefore see the force of the argument advanced by the sponsor of the -bill for British fair play in allowing the bill to go before the special committee previous to its discussion in this House. It seems to me that the promotors have had a good deal of British fair play in having this charter renewed thirteen or fourteen times, and now that they come to the House for another renewal I for one do not feel disposed to grant it unless good reasons can be advanced for so doing. So far we have had no reasons at all, except such as were given this afternoon in the address of the hon. member for Nipissing, an address which can be answered in a very few moments. That 
hon. gentleman dealt almost exclusively with the construction of the canal. If these people who are seeking a renewal of the charter would confine the charter solely to the building of the Georgian bay canal, I do not think they would experience that difficulty in getting the bill through the House which they are having at the present time, notwithstanding the fact that there are many members of this House who are committed to the principle of having canals owned and operated by -the government rather than by private interests. I think it is almost too late in the day for people to ask this House to give [DOT]them the right to levy tolls on ships which are to pass through canals built in this Dominion. Allowing private companies to develop such public utilities is entirely contrary to the past policy of governments of whatever party they may be composed. To me, however, the main principle involved in this bill, and which I feel bound to oppose, is the granting to a private corporation the right to own and control almost one and a quarter million horse-power on the Ottawa river. When the charter was originally granted there was no idea then of the value of electrical energy, but since then a tremendous development in this direction has taken place. Science has made enormous strides, so that what was impossible only five or ten years ago is practicable to-day. For instance, there was a time when long distance transmission as we now have it was almost impossible. To-day we transmit electrical energy over a distance of 100 miles with comparatively little loss in energy. I find in to-day's newspaper a small item which in my opinion has considerable significance in relation to this particular charter. I believe that these falls are situated about 300 miles from the large centres of population in Ontario. At present it would be almost impossible from an engineering standpoint to transmit that electrical energy over that distance, -but, as I say, science is making rapid progress, and I myself expect to see in the next few years such an evolution in electrical engineering as will render possible the transmission of power from Georgian bay to the city of Toronto. In this morning's Ottawa Citizen I find this despatch by the Canadian Press:
Toronto, Ont. March 5.-A New York despatch to the Mail and Empire says: A new invention which makes possible the economical transmission of power from distant waterfalls and will soon permit scattered districts and farms, almost anywhere in the country to be supplied with power, was announced to-day by W. S. Rugg, vice-president in charge of engineering of the Westingliouse Electric and Manufacturing Company. Mr. Rugg said the

Georgian Day Canal Company
invention by Frank G. Baum, hydro-electrical engineer, of San Francisco, was a complete solution of the problem of economical transmission of power over long distances.
With the imminent solution of the problem of transmitting electrical energy over long distances one can visualize the tremendous importance of the water-powers on the Ottawa river, when.there is a million and a quarter horse-power there to be developed. Personally I am strongly opposed to this bill, particularly now when I find that the people of Ontario are themselves prepared to proceed with the development of this horsepower if they have an opportunity of doing so.
It seems to me rather strange that there should be hon. gentlemen in this House from the province of Ontario who would rather trust their destinies to people who, on thirteen or fourteen different occasions, have failed them, than to the provincial government who have built and developed one of the finest hydro-electric enterprises to be found anywhere in the universe. If there is in Ontario to-day approximately 600,000 horse-power available for development, the first people who should have an opportunity of using that horse-power are the people of Ontario themselves, and this House of Commons at least should do nothing in this matter before the people of the province have been consulted.
This morning, along with other members, I received a circular from the Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company in which I was rather interested. Unlike many other hon, members, I had no lobbyists here to see me on this particular question and when I received the circular I was interested to know what they had to say about the development of the potential horse-power on the Ottawa river. Yet in a three-page circular sent out by the company not a word is said about this power development; the circular is confined to the canal. It is somewhat strange that they should so completely ignore the power aspect of this enterprise and emphasize the future activities of the canal. It is my candid opinion that even if the charter is granted the people of northern Ontario will never have a canal if they depend on this company. There is a question, however, as to whether they are going to get something if the charter is not granted and the power rights are handed over to the people of Ontario. Personally I believe the Dominion government to be fairly well committed on this point, and in that connection I wish to read one or two extracts from Hansard from a debate which took place last year. The House will remember that last
session the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) moved a resolution which read as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, measures should be taken to regain for the use of the people the coal mines and water-powers which are now being exploited in the interest of private corporations rather than for the needs of the people.
The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) was very sympathetic to this resolution and so expressed himself in the following words:
The provincial governments, with the exception of the three prairie provinces, own and control their forest wealth. In my attempt to get uniformity of action I found a great deal of suspicion abroad in the minds of the provincial authorities, and I admit that the feeling is sometimes too prevalent that there is a desire on the part of the federal authorities to interfere with provincial rights.
The same thing would also apply to power rights, and the minister said further:
One of the first difficulties is that under the Act of Confederation those public utilities which are mentioned in the resolution remain under the control of the provincial government.
If the speech of the hon. gentleman is read through several references will be found to show that the control and practically the ownership of these water rights are absolutely under the jurisdiction of the provinces. Consequently when the question of the development of this water-power is considered, I do not think this House has the absolute right to give away something which is admitted by many to be entirely within the jurisdiction of the provinces.
To go a point further, I find that in Ontario the Hydro Electric Commission has developed approximately SOO.OOO horse-power at an approximate cost of $240,000,000, and I think that when the people of Ontario have shown so much initiative in this development and when they have spent so much money in developing this tremendous asset, in giving lower rates than can be obtained in any other part of the continent, this House should not lightly pass a bill giving a private company the right to develop almost an equal quantity of electrical energy. There is admittedly a shortage of power in Ontario; the provincial government wants more power developed. If we look at the record of the speeches made when a resolution dealing with the shortage of power in Ontario was introduced by the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) and seconded by Mr. Maclean, who was then a member of the House, we will find further references by ministers of the crown to the right of Ontario to control and own whatever water-power may be developed in the province.

Georgian Bay Canal Company
I think we should have a pronouncement on this question by the government; I think the matter too important to put the responsibility on one private member. In view of their past statements I do not think the government should altogether leave the responsibility to the House; I think they should take a stand on this question and let us know their decision. When the people of the largest province in Canada are applying themselves to the development of their water-powers, [with all political parties united, I do not think this parliament can honestly give those powers away to any private corporation. Therefore I think the government should say where they stand on this question, and I hope they are in favour of giving to the people of Ontario that which belongs to them.
In the development of some of its publie-owned utilities Canada has one of its greatest assets. Just the other day in this House the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Bell), in speaking on the budget, made a most pathetic plea on behalf of a private corporation, the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company, and at this juncture I would like to say a few words in connection with what was then said. His plea was that this poor company which is conferring such vast benefits iipon the people of Montreal-and which incidentally earns such huge dividends-should be relieved of the payment of income tax amounting to approximately $750,000 yearly. In the remarks of the hon. member we find the difference between those who favour public ownership and those who believe in private ownership. The hon. member who spoke for the company probably thought the company could pay larger dividends if this income tax were not paid, as in the case of a publicly owned utility. We find that in Ontario they give a rate as low as can be found in the world, and this is in my opinion one of the greatest assets to our manufacturers. In Ontario I believe electrical energy can be bought for industrial purposes at three-quarters of a cent per kilowatt hour, while in the city of Winnipeg under our municipally-owned hydro-electric system electrical energy is sold for industrial purposes for as little as two-fifths of a cent per kilowatt hour. That is almost below the cost of production, but with the large off-peak load which exists there, we have been able to make that tremendous concession to consumers of large blocks of electrical energy. The other night the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) stated that the electrical heating of our homes would soon become possible through the further development of electrical energy. He 
was not looking very far ahead, because I can tell the House that at the present time electric heating is being done in the city of Winnipeg to a very large extent. I desire to mention these facts, Mr. Speaker, because it shows the great potential value of the power development with which the House is dealing at present. In Winnipeg we have a central heating system owned and controlled 'by the city, which was put in as an adjunct to a stand-by plant which is necessary to our hydro-electric system. During certain months of the year this central heating system does not consume one ounce of coal; the off-peak electric power is developed into steam through electrically heated boilers and by a high pressure system the steam is put through the mains and the larger portion of the business section of Winnipeg is heated in that way. During probably two or three months of the year, therefore, no coal at all is used to heat the central business portion of Winnipeg. Consequently the statement made here by the hon. member for Argenteuil that this is something not likely to happen in the years to come is met by the assertion that it is an accomplished fact so far as one city on this continent is concerned, and the example of that city will prdbably be copied by others. I am satisfied that before very long Toronto will establish a stand-by plant in connection with its own hydro-electric system, and when it does there is nothing more economical it can do than to combine that stand-by plant with a central heating system. We shall probably see in the near future a large portion of the central part of Toronto heated by the off-peak load of its hydro-electric system the same as is done in the city of Winnipeg.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before
recess I was dealing with a question that was raised by the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) who had visualized the utilization of electrical energy for heating purposes. I had dealt for a few moments with the fact that in the city of Winnipeg that vision had already become a reality, and that we were now using electrical energy for the development of heat. During the recess I was asked by one or two hon. members to deal for a few moments longer with that particular matter, and without taking up too much of the time of the House, I wish, in

Georgian Bay Canal Company
order to satisfy the request made by the hon. gentlemen, to give a few more details in regard to that particular aspect.
In the development of any hydro-electric enterprise there is bound to be a large off-peak load which is like a by-product and is bound to go to waste. I do not think in the Dominion of Canada the average consumption over a twenty-four-hour period exceeds fifty per cent of the total quantity of electrical energy generated, the result being that there is a fifty per cent off-peak load that goes almost entirely to waste. It has always been a problem with electrical engineers how to utilize that waste in hydro-electric development1, and in the city of Winnipeg we have come as close as any other city to the utilization of that off-peak load or the by-product of hydro-electric development.
That has been effected in this way. In Winnipeg we were bound by circumstances to erect a stand-by plant for our hydro-electric system. That stand-by plant became necessary, as I believe it will become necessary in all large centres where large quantities of electrical energy are used, owing to the fact that at certain periods of the year cyclonic storms would blow down the transmission lines or there would be a stoppage from other causes, with the result that there would be very little or no hydro-electric energy obtainable in the city to carry on essential public utilities and works in factories such as packing plants and so forth. Hospitals would probably be without electrical energy; elevators in hospitals would be unable to run and so on, and the commercial life of the city would be completely demoralized for the time being. With the creation of a stand-by or auxiliary plant, as some people call it, we are able to give to a large section of the users of hydro-electric energy in Winnipeg a guaranteed twenty-four-hour continuous service.
The erection of such a stand-by plant involves a very large capital outlay as well as a large annual outlay for upkeep. One of the methods used to keep down that expenditure was the creation of a joint utility by combining with the stand-by plant a central heating system whereby the boilers, which are kept in readiness to generate electricity in case of emergency, can be utilized for heating purposes. What we do now is to generate heat through these boilers in the winter time; but in addition to that we have certain electric boilers, which are made in Canada, which were made by Canadian engineers, and the off-peak power which is on tap for many months in the year and for many hours each day finds its way into these 32649-61
electrical boilers. These boilers, which have a capacity of 750 horse-power and are not much larger than one of the desks in this chamber, generate steam which is sold in exactly the same way as steam that is produced by the use of coal. That brings in a large revenue to the city by using hydroelectric eneigy which otherwise would go to waste.
We have partly solved another problem which I believe is seeking solution in many other parts of the Dominion. More than one hundred of the largest buildings in the centre of Winnipeg are now supplied with heat from a central heating plant, and in the milder winter weather such as we have at the present time and such as they had in Winnipeg during February, not one ounce of coal is used for the creation of heat. The result is that in months where in other cities they have vast volumes of smoke coming out of their chimneys, Winnipeg is almost a smokeless city so that the atmosphere there possesses advantages that are not possessed by other cities. Moreover users of electrical energy in Winnipeg who find it essential to have a twenty-four-hour continuous service receive that by the creation of the stand-by plant which was put into operation, I believe, in 1924. I have endeavoured to make these one or two points clear for the bnefit of hon. members who asked me the question during the recess; otherwise, I had no intention of dealing again with the matter.
Coming back to the direct question of the bill before the House, another objection I have to it is the fact that if the charter is granted to the people who are seeking it there will be established in Ontario something which I believe will not be to the advantage of that province. It would mean for the province a dual system of private ownership and public ownership. Whilst I know that many hon. members will say that competition is a good thing, I believe an monopolies in certain things. I think the control of electric energy should be a monopoly and already in Ontario, 'the hydro-electric commission have a monopoly practically of this service which they give to the people. I think it would therefore be unfair of parliament to establish another system to enter into competition to a certain extent with the already publicly-owned utility of the province of Ontario. I have no doubt in my own mind that such a corporation should not come into competition, although I have an idea that if the power were granted to them they might hold up this charter and try to bargain with someone who would give them a good price for it. What is



Georgian Bay Canal Company
likely to be the result if a charter is granted? I understand that they could tap a region already not tapped by the Ontario Hydro Electric Commission. If they put into operation a hydro-electric system in the province, and then started supplying the people of those areas with electric light and power, I am satisfied that they would have to charge a much larger price than is charged to the people who use the energy of the publicly-owned utility of Ontario.
The 'hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Lapierre), When speaking this afternoon, said the canal system would have to be carried by profits of the power operation. I noted that statement when he made it, and I think what he meant was that the promoters of the bill would charge the users of electric energy in the area they would serve, a much larger price than they would ordinarily charge, and would be able to put the canal system into operation by tfhe profits they would make out of the hydro-electric system. I think, Mr. Speaker, that is a very false position for any one in this House to fake. There is no canal system in this country which is now being paid for by a.ny auxiliary company. There are no canal tolls in effect at the present time, and it would be a mistake for us to give a company the right, as we would be doing under this charter, to charge more for electric liigjht and power in order that it might be able to subsidize a canal system which it has in contemplation.
Discussing the question of rates brings me again to the point raised by the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Bell) the other night when he was speaking about rates. I think I asked a question in reference to the rates as between a privately-owned corporation and a publicly-owned utility, and he was good enough to reply by quoting from the annual statement of the company in which they said that t)he average retail rate in the city of Montreal was three and a half cents a kilowatt hour. I think that statement will be found in Hansard. If we take the rate charged in other cities where they (have hydro-electric enterprises under public ownership, we see quite a difference. The average retail rate charged in the city of Winnipeg, with which I am familiar, would not be more than two cents a kilowatt hour. Making all allowances,
I think the rates charged in Montreal are fully fifty per cent higher than those charged in Winnipeg. I believe, without having before me the actual facts, that the same ratio would apply to Toronto and other large cities. In that same connection, the hon. member was urging that the company known as the 
Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company should be relieved of its annual income tax payment, amounting to slightly over three quarters of a million dollars; that it was an injustice to the company, and that they ought to be relieved of the payment, on the ground that a publicly-owned utility is not required to pay income tax to the national exchequer. The people of the province of Quebec have a simple way of equalizing matters; all they have to do is to own the utilities, as they do in Ontario; then they will have no tax to pay. That is one way of overcoming the difficulty, if they wish to do it. I do not think they should penalize a public utility because in Quebec they have private ownership. In this particular regard I want to quote a very brief synopsis of the statement made in the annual report of the company. I am quoting from the Financial Times of January 28th, and hon. members will see in what poor circumstances this particular company as. The report says:
Gross revenue from operations for the year 1926, is $18,907,382, compared with $18,346,806 for the year 1925, and $17,394,091 for the year 1924. A favorable feature is a reduction in operating expenses and taxes during the year.
My hon. friend from St. Antoine is not satisfied with the ordinary tax reduction, but he is willing to give them about three-quarters of a million in addition. *
The former being down at $7,109,918 from $7,349,243, and the latter down at $1,213,028 from $1,274,655, while appropriation for depreciation is up at $1,890,738 from $1,834,880.
But that is not all. I want to give the House a few more figures.
Net revenue shows a gain of over $800,000, at $8,693,688 as compared with $7,890,026. Respecting the issue during the year of $30,000,000 of bonds is an increase in fixed charges to $1,611,121 from $1,213,650.
And I think we know what these figures are. They are a melon cut for the shareholders.
Leaving net earnings available for dividends on the 2,041,837 shares of capital stock outstanding at $7,082,567, or the equivalent of $3.47 a share; this compares with net earnings of $6,676,376 for the year 1925, equal to 10.32 per cent, (or $3.44 per share figured on the basis of the recent 3 for 1 split).
I think we all have an idea what is meant by the three for one split, and this corporation split their shares three for one.
Dividends absorbed the sum of $5,135,041 as compared with $5,119,091 in 1925, and surplus for the year at $1,869,482, compares with $1,537,285.

Georgian Bay Canal Company
Now, Mr. Speaker, a public-owned utility does not publish balance sheets of this character, it does not split up shares three to one. Instead of paying cash dividends out of surpluses, the public-owned utility gives its customers reduced rates and better service. Therefore the people of Toronto and Winnipeg and other large centres where these publicly-owned utilities are operating get the benefit of rates which are about fifty per cent lower than those prevailing in, say, Montreal, and probably in other cities throughout the province of Quebec. But the communities where public-owned utilities are operating have a further advantage. Probably there is not a city on the North American continent where on the basis of population as much electricity is used as in Winnipeg. There we try to bring it into the homes of all the people. We try to make the lot of the housewife easier, and in the average household in Winnipeg you will find an electric stove and other equipment, all of which lightens the work of the housewife and improves the conditions of the home. I can say of my own knowledge that private ownership never displayed the initiative that is so conspicuous Tinder public ownership in the city of Winnipeg.
I have another objection to the bill. As a layman, I take it that the bill gives to the company a perpetual franchise. I believe there is a clause somewhere, perhaps in the old bill, which gives to the government the right of expropriation. I have some idea of what expropriation proceedings are, and I can understand how7 much a private corporation would demand for surrendering a perpetual franchise; the amount required would be staggering. So I cannot for the life of me see why we should give to a private corporation these valuable privileges and at a subsequent period buy them back for millions and millions of dollars. Undoubtedly the safest course will be to see that the promoters do not get a renewal of this franchise, and thus save ourselves the expense of expropriating their franchise at a later period. But I am asked by those who are sponsoring this bill, "Why not send it to the committee and discuss it there?" I do not see the reasonableness of myself and others who are opposed to the bill being required to go before the committee with our objections. I believe it is the safer policy to express my opinion now on the floor of the house and show where I stand, rather than wTait until the bill comes back from the committee after having received its second reading.
In dealing with this question I think we ought to take into consideration, Sir, the fact 32649-61J	,
that the legislature of Ontario is to-day discussing this identical question and, according to newspapers, a resolution is to be framed in such a way as to meet the wishes of all parties there-the conservative party, the liberal party, the progressive party and the labour party. They will all unite on a resolution asking this parliament to preserve the rights which belong to the province. In view of this we ought to pause a long time before we do anything which would in any way infringe on the rights of Ontario and give to a private corporation something which really belongs to the people of that province.
It has been argued by those who are promoting -this bill that the province of Quebec may give the water-powers on the Ottawa river over to private ownership for development. Well, if the government of Quebec favours private ownership development, that is the business of the people of that province. On the other hand, if the people of Ontario want to develop their share of these water-powers under public ownership, then they ought to be given the opportunity of doing so as part of their hydro-electric system. I believe that within the Liberal party there are quite a number of members who are in favour of the principle of public ownership, particularly those from western Canada. It is only quite recently that at a convention the Liberal party in Manitoba went on record as being in favour of the public ownership and operation of water-powers. I hope the Liberal members representing Manitoba in this house will fbllow the lead of the provincial party convention and help to uphold the principle of public ownership of utilities not only in Manitoba but in Ontario, for after all what is good in the one province is good in the other. I oppose this bill mainly on the ground that it is a complete violation of the principles of public ownership; further, I oppose it because I believe that the people of Ontario are anxious to retain these water-powers in order to develop them in the interests of the whole province. I believe, Sir, that when the interests of a small group of capitalists-of men who are attempting to exploit the people of Ontario and their rights-are opposing the interests of the people of that province, I as a member of this house must decide in favour of the people of Ontario.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this House ought aa far as possible to conserve the rights of the people in the development of their natural resources, and when we find that Ontario, through its premier, through the members of its legislature, and through other authorities in a position to speak, has expressed in most

Georgian Bay Canal Company
emphatic terms that it would be a great injustice to the people of Ontario if we renewed this franchise, it seems to me that the only course open to us is to see that this bill is not allowed to pass. It has been before the house on fourteen different occasions, and for thirty-three years its promoters have enjoyed the privileges and rights which they now seek to have renewed, but during all that time they have done nothing to carry out the project for which in the first instance the charter was ostensibly granted them. Therefore, Sir, I think we shall be acting in the best interests of the people of Ontario by rejecting this bill1 and thus allowing the provincial authorities to develop their own natural resources.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon.
member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) and the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) that it is highly desirable to have a full discussion of this measure before referring it to the committee. There are two questions involved in the renewal: first, the construction of what is called the Georgian bay canal, and second, the development of the water-power along the route, including the development of the power on the Ottawa river. I do not propose to discuss the various legal questions involved, nor to discuss the respective powers of the Dominion of Canada, on the one hand, and the provinces of Ontario and Quebec on the other. We have courts properly constituted and competent to decide questions of this sort. If Canada has no jurisdiction in the matter of granting this charter, then, I submit, Canada can do itself no harm in granting it. Let us assume that Canada has the power to grant it and let us endeavour to discuss the question from the point of view of the principles involved.
The hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. La-pierre) made it quite clear, in my opinion, that the canal in question cannot be economically constructed or operated except in conjunction with the development of the water-power along the canal route. The two, in my opinion, ought not to be separated. But we should be careful to draw this distinction. The canal cannot be operated as a commercial undertaking without at the same time developing the water-power; but, on the other hand, it is possible to develop the water-power without building the canal. I think that distinction ought to be clearly kept in mind.
I listened with -a great deal of interest to the remarks of the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). It might be prefer-

able that this whole scheme should be undertaken by the Dominion. I should be inclined personally to favour such a proposal, but I do not believe that such a scheme would be undertaken. Water-power, we are frequently told, is one of our greatest assets and it should be jealously guarded by the people of Canada. But it is not an asset until it is developed. If we have to choose, in the development of our water-power, between Dominion control and private enterprise, then I think the remarks of the hon. member for North Winnipeg are well founded. [DOT] But if it is not probable-and it does not seem to be probable-that the Dominion will undertake this project as a public ownership scheme, then I think we shall have to choose between two methods of water-power development: on the one hand, a scheme of water-power development that will bring with it cheap transportation and, on the other, a scheme that brings no transportation facilities at all. That point, I think, is worthy of the consideration of the House, and, personally, I should much prefer a scheme of water-power development that carries with it the possibilities of cheap transportation to a scheme that offers no transportation facilities at all.
I quite agree with the various speakers who have pointed out that great care must be taken by the House in transferring waterpower sites to private individuals or even to provinces. As I understand it, under the statutes that have been passed, relating to the Georgian bay canal, since the year 1894 when this company was incorporated, the rights of the public are very fully protected. I understand that the Dominion will have complete control over the construction and operation of the canal, over the levying of tolls, and over the sale of water-power. Furthermore, I understand that it is competent for the Dominion to take over the whole scheme at any time. I fully agree with other speakers that our great assets should be adequately safeguarded, and if there are not adequate safeguards provided in the present statutes relating to this corporation, then those safeguards should now be set up as a condition precedent to the renewal of the charter.
Those who are in favour of the Georgian bay canal project point out its many advantages not only to western Canada but to eastern and central Canada as well. The Georgian bay canal will establish a deep waterway from Montreal to Fort William and Port Arthur and it will be an all-Canadian deep waterway. Those who speak in its support say that it will industrialize the whole Ottawa valley. They say that it will increase the development of the port of Montreal and of

Groryian Bay Canal Company
all the cities on the lower St. Lawrence. The hon. member for Tort William (Mr. Manion) in his speech this afternoon emphasized the value of the St. Lawrence waterway. So far as I can see, all advantages which he pointed out as accruing from the St. Lawrence waterway scheme will flow from the Georgian bay canal undertaking. In addition the friends of the Georgian bay canal point out that it will provide cheap transportation from the maritime provinces as far west as Fort William. They argue that it will provide cheap transportation for Nova Scotia coal to Ontario, that it will open up the mining area of the latter province, and that it will enable ore to be carried cheaply to Cape Breton where the coal supply is situated.
